office: Ward One Member of the Council of the District of Columbia
scope_plain: Only Ward 1 voters. Ranked choice: four candidates plus a write-in line, so you can rank up to 5. Rank as many or as few as you like; ranking more never hurts your first choice.
office_explainer: Your ward's one seat on the 13-member DC Council, which writes city laws and passes the budget.
why_it_matters: Open seat: Brianne Nadeau, first elected in 2014, is not running. The winner represents Adams Morgan, Columbia Heights, Mount Pleasant and nearby neighborhoods. Democrat Aparna Raj won a five-way June primary with 52% in the final ranked-choice round.

candidates.name: Jett James Jasper
candidates.background: Nonprofit executive and community leader. His party profile says he has led nonprofit and private-sector organizations, served on local boards and commissions, and worked in hospitality and public access media.

own_words.text: DC GOP profile: running "with a focus on public safety, affordability, small business support, and ensuring government works effectively for residents."

candidates.name: Ryan Prince
candidates.background: Independent candidate. Qualified for the ballot by petition (picked up petitions June 15, filed August 5, 2026, per DCBOE).

candidates.name: Jude Crannitch
candidates.background: The DC Statehood Green Party's nominee for Ward 1; won the party's June primary unopposed.

own_words.text: Champions "wage justice, green democracy, and a cultural renaissance" for Ward 1 (party profile).
Party profile says he is committed to D.C. statehood and stronger neighborhood representation.

candidates.name: Aparna Raj
candidates.background: Tenant organizer and former chair of Metro DC Democratic Socialists of America. Won the June 16 Democratic primary with 52.3% in the final round.

own_words.text: "I will fight to expand rent stabilization to cover all multifamily properties."
Would legalize apartments in every neighborhood, end minimum parking requirements for new buildings, and make at least one-third of new homes affordable.
On slow bus upgrades for U St and Georgia Ave: "Bus riders should not have to wait six years for improvements to service quality."

scope_plain: Only Ward 3 voters. Pick one. One candidate plus a write-in line.

candidates.name: Matthew Frumin
candidates.background: Ward 3 councilmember since 2023 and an attorney. Before the Council he served on his local ANC and worked on affordable housing with the Washington Interfaith Network. Won the June primary unopposed.

own_words.text: "I support adding housing on our commercial and transit corridors – Connecticut and Wisconsin Avenues as examples."
Says he is "not there" on ending single-family zoning, and opposes eliminating parking minimums, preferring case-by-case waivers.
"I would like to see aggressive implementation of the STEER Act to hold serial offenders accountable."

office: Ward Five Member of the Council of the District of Columbia
scope_plain: Only Ward 5 voters. Ranked choice: three candidates plus a write-in line, so you can rank up to 4. Rank as many or as few as you like.
office_explainer: Your ward's one seat on the 13-member DC Council, which writes city laws and passes the budget.
why_it_matters: Zachary Parker, first elected in 2022, is seeking a second term representing much of Northeast DC. He won the June Democratic primary with 78% against two challengers.

candidates.name: Zachary Parker
candidates.background: Ward 5 councilmember since 2023; previously served on the DC State Board of Education. Won the June primary with 77.6%.

own_words.text: "At least 50% of new units should be income restricted to expand deeply affordable housing."

"I was proud to co introduce the STEER Act to hold reckless drivers accountable."

candidates.background: DC Statehood Green Party steering committee member and the party's Ward 5 nominee; won its June primary unopposed.

own_words.text: Champions "economic justice, green democracy, and policies that prioritize people over profit" (party profile).
Party profile says she works to strengthen community representation and advance D.C. statehood.

candidates.name: Jeffrey Kihien-Palza
candidates.background: Peruvian immigrant and longtime Ward 5 resident. His party profile describes him as a business leader and attorney who has led G & K Management LLC for over 15 years.

own_words.text: DC GOP profile: focused on "strengthening neighborhoods, supporting economic opportunity, and serving Ward 5 residents."

candidates.name: Charles Allen
candidates.background: Ward 6 councilmember since 2015 (three terms) and chair of the Council's Committee on Transportation and the Environment. Won the June primary with 75.7%.

own_words.text: Says he "authored the landmark STEER Act to increase accountability for dangerous drivers."
"I created the District's first e-bike voucher program."

Top transportation priority: "Improving pedestrian and cyclist safety at high-injury intersections."
"Leadership starts with listening."

scope_plain: You vote in one ANC race: the one for your own single-member district (SMD), about 2,000 neighbors. Ward 1 has 42 SMDs in ANCs 1A to 1E. Of those, 32 have one candidate, 7 have two, 2 have three or more and use ranked choice (1B03, 1E02), and 1 has no one on the ballot, only a write-in line (1A02).
office_explainer: Your unpaid neighborhood rep for about 2,000 residents. Advises the city on liquor licenses, zoning, traffic and parking.
why_it_matters: ANCs are the closest government gets to your front door: the first stop for a new bar's liquor license, a zoning request or a traffic-safety fix. City agencies are required to give their recommendations special consideration.
anc_explainer: What it is: DC is cut into 345 single-member districts (SMDs) of about 2,000 people each. Each SMD elects one Advisory Neighborhood Commissioner. The SMDs are grouped into 46 commissions.
What they do: weigh in on liquor licenses, zoning and building plans, traffic, parking, trash, policing and the city budget. They advise; they cannot pass laws.
Why it matters: city agencies are required to give their recommendations special consideration, so your commissioner's vote can shape a new bar, building or bike lane on your block.
The job: a two-year term with no salary.

On your ballot: exactly one ANC race, for your own SMD, near the end, just before Initiative 86. Many have one candidate, some have none (only a write-in line), and races with three or more candidates use ranked choice.
Find yours: look up your address in the city's ANC locator. Your SMD code (like 1B05) starts with your ward number. Two commissions cross ward lines: 3/4G (Wards 3 and 4) and 6/8F (Wards 6 and 8).

how_to_find_yours.text: Enter your address in the city's ANC locator to get your SMD code, then find that code below. Your mailed ballot also prints your ANC race.

office_explainer: Your unpaid neighborhood rep for about 2,000 residents. Advises the city on liquor licenses, zoning, traffic and parking.
why_it_matters: ANCs are the closest government gets to your front door: the first stop for a new bar's liquor license, a zoning request or a traffic-safety fix. City agencies are required to give their recommendations special consideration.
anc_explainer: What it is: DC is cut into 345 single-member districts (SMDs) of about 2,000 people each. Each SMD elects one Advisory Neighborhood Commissioner. The SMDs are grouped into 46 commissions.
What they do: weigh in on liquor licenses, zoning and building plans, traffic, parking, trash, policing and the city budget. They advise; they cannot pass laws.
Why it matters: city agencies are required to give their recommendations special consideration, so your commissioner's vote can shape a new bar, building or bike lane on your block.
The job: a two-year term with no salary.

On your ballot: exactly one ANC race, for your own SMD, near the end, just before Initiative 86. Many have one candidate, some have none (only a write-in line), and races with three or more candidates use ranked choice.
Find yours: look up your address in the city's ANC locator. Your SMD code (like 1B05) starts with your ward number. Two commissions cross ward lines: 3/4G (Wards 3 and 4) and 6/8F (Wards 6 and 8).
